text:
The 8GB 480 is far too expensive in the UK compared to the 4GB model, so it's not really worth considering. The difficult choice for me is between the 8GB 470 and the 4GB 480. You can get the MSI Gaming X version of both on Overclockers right now for the exact same price (£218.99)

Would you say the 10% or so extra performance is more valuable than the possible future-proofing from the extra RAM? Right now I'm edging towards the 4GB 480 but it doesn't seem like an obvious choice to me. 8GB is excessive, especially on a card that will see general performance issues long before it can use that amount, but on the other hand I'm not overly comfortable with 4GB. The 6GB on the GTX1060 seems like the perfect amount for this price range really, but unfortunately the aftermarket versions of those are ridiculously overpriced, so it's not really an option for me.

Would love any extra opinions, been trying to decide between these and the 1060 for a good two weeks.
author: @kubeface115

text:
That's my thinking too. Right now 3-4GB is more than enough for the majority of decently optimized games at 1080p, but I'm not sure it will be in 1-2 years. Still, it seems like the better option, since turning texture quality down a notch is preferable to lacking general horsepower.

I wish I could replace hardware as soon as it becomes obsolete, but sadly I'm a peasant, so longevity is somewhat of a concern.
author: @kubeface115

text:
Yeah, you're probably right. The only real exceptions seem to be heavy mod use (e.g. Skyrim texture packs), badly optimised games and games with ridiculous settings that were never really intended to be used by the average gamer.

I was actually shocked at how little vram Witcher 3 used. It tends to stay around 2GB or under at 1080p and even at 4k only goes to around 3GB. Pretty damn impressive considering how gorgeous it looks.

Thanks for the second opinion!

text: Hiebly no they're not, they do as much as AMD does. Look at the 7850 which was a cut down 7870, same concept, but there was a little performance gap. Until the 10xx series, the usual run was a cut down card like the 670/970 could be overclocked to the same performance of a stock 680/980, while there was a $200 price difference (not worth it). Now with the 1080, you get a lot of performance gain for the price you pay. It also goes hand in hand with the fab process. Imperfections means they have to blast those dead cores off. It's harder to get a chip with 3000+ cudas on it to not have many when the cores are so small. By the 1070 having less cores they will have more chips that are able to be put in 1070s. So there are multiple sides.

author: @mysticjbyrd

text:
Because they're both based on exactly the same chip. The 480 has everything enabled while the 470 has parts of it disabled.

GPU (and CPU) manufacturers do this because every new chip is incredibly expensive to develop and they simply can't afford to create a whole load of unique chips for every new architecture. However they don't just disable completely functional parts, they often also sell partially defective chips with the defective parts disabled meaning that they can still get money from chips that would have ended up being recycled or just thrown in the trash.
author: @LAG09

text:
Chiriac Puiu 470s aren't low binned 480s, they are imperfect 480s that required some of the compute units turned off.  

Some of them might actually be perfectly functional 480s that had parts disabled.  It's happened in the past.  For instance, some people were able to flash a 290 to a 290x.
